analysis.one_liner: Made it much harder for federal judges to throw out civil lawsuits before evidence is gathered.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had a Democratic sponsor and 36 cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in December 2009, and died there without a vote when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2007 and 2009, Supreme Court decisions (Ashcroft v. Iqbal and Bell Atlantic v. Twombly) let federal judges dismiss a lawsuit at the start if the complaint didn't seem "plausible" — before the plaintiff could gather any evidence. This bill wrote the older standard into federal law instead: a case could only be dismissed if it appeared beyond doubt that no set of facts could support the claim. That would have let many discrimination, consumer, and injury cases against companies and officials get past the first hurdle and into the evidence-gathering stage, instead of ending on a judge's early guess about the facts.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who sue — employees claiming discrimination, consumers, patients, and people injured by companies or government officials — who today often see their cases dismissed before they can present evidence, because a judge finds their complaint not "plausible" on its face.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Civil rights, consumer, and injury plaintiffs

how_it_helps.text: Bars a federal court from dismissing a complaint unless it appears beyond doubt that the plaintiff can prove no set of facts supporting the claim.

Bars judges from dismissing a complaint merely because the judge finds its factual allegations not "plausible" or not enough to reasonably infer the defendant is liable — the standards the Supreme Court adopted in Twombly (2007) and Iqbal (2009).

In practice this restores the pre-2007 "notice pleading" regime, under which a case could only be thrown out at the start in extreme cases, giving plaintiffs access to discovery (the process of collecting evidence from the other side).

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and institutions being sued — corporations, insurers, banks, employers, and government defendants — who would face more lawsuits surviving early dismissal and reaching discovery, which raises defense costs and settlement pressure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate and government defendants in lawsuits

drawbacks.text: The old "no set of facts" standard lets weak or meritless lawsuits survive to discovery, which is expensive for defendants to defend and can pressure settlements — this is the core objection businesses and defense lawyers raised to rolling back the plausibility standard.

The bill would write one pleading rule directly into federal statute, overriding decisions reached through the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure process run by the judiciary (the bill allows later rule changes only through that formal process).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with real claims, the bill removed a barrier that ends many lawsuits before any evidence can be collected — a judge's early plausibility judgment, made without discovery, often gets the facts wrong. The honest cost is that weaker cases would also get through to expensive discovery, raising litigation costs for defendants and potentially driving some settlements. Whether that trade is worth it is the crux of a long-running debate; the bill itself never advanced far enough for that debate to happen in Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its Courts and Competition Policy subcommittee, which held one hearing in December 2009 — and the bill never got a committee vote, a floor vote, or any action afterward before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 19, 2009 by Rep. Jerrold Nadler with ten original co-introducers and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On December 11, 2009 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts and Competition Policy.
The subcommittee held a hearing on December 16, 2009; that was the last action of any kind on the bill.
The bill gathered 36 cosponsors (35 Democrats, 1 Republican) but was never reported out of committee and never received a vote in the House before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses and other frequent defendants in federal court — employers, insurers, banks, and government agencies — are better off, because they keep the plausibility standard that lets them get lawsuits dismissed early, before discovery costs mount. The bill's supporters' effort produced only a hearing.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.role: House Judiciary Committee member; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the pre-2007 pleading standard in federal courts.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers
for.what_they_did: Joined Nadler as an original co-introducer of the bill, whose referral went to the committee he chaired.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or reported it to the House floor after the December 2009 subcommittee hearing; no further action was taken for over a year.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business community
against.what_they_did: Fought to preserve the Twombly/Iqbal plausibility pleading standard, which they credit with screening out weak lawsuits and reducing litigation costs.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic: 35 of 253 House Democrats cosponsored, alongside a single House Republican, and the bill never reached a vote where the split could be counted.

industries.industry: Corporate and institutional litigation defendants (employers, insurers, banks, government agencies)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped away the plausibility standard those defendants use to dismiss many lawsuits at the outset, forcing more cases into costly discovery. Their interest in easy early dismissal runs against plaintiffs' interest in having claims heard on the evidence.
More cases surviving dismissal means more work for lawyers representing consumers, employees, and injury victims — and their income depends on the same access to court their clients need.
